utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Just a couple very quick points before we begin. I checked the transcript we admitted as the witness's 92 ter statement and there were on two days several pages of testimony that was not in open session, so it may be best to leave two versions, it may be simplest. Second, I noticed an error when I was reading the transcript. On page 22064, last sentence: "How long was the video as you remember it?" Should be: "How long was the meeting as you remember it?" I also wanted to let the Chamber and the parties know that I spoke to Mr. Robinson that we're having some difficulties obtaining Dutch interpreters for the next two days and we're working on that and we'll try to resolve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question is: We do need the Dutch translators for the other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we've checked that. And I just wanted to let everybody know that our estimate for expert Wright will be a little bit longer than we put in our notification because he's the first expert to explain the way these things worked, the direct will be a little bit longer than we estimated just to let everybody know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Boering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Boering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told, Mr. Karadzic, that you have 40 minutes for today with Mr. Boering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, you said you had not seen Serb soldiers in a long time and it was necessary for somebody from the 28th Division to point them out. Why was that? When you were making the decision or when the decision was being made about close support or air support, your dilemma was about the whereabouts of the Serb troops and you had to order strikes. Why did you need to know their location? Did you also need to see them with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time that in the enclave attacks were taking place from the outside on to the enclave and the population was withdrawing on to Srebrenica city itself. There were -- there was fire and violence from the outside in. And there was also the withdrawal of DutchBat and of Muslim fighters. To nevertheless attempt to try and call a halt to these things, naturally a defence was needed that would keep and to be able to defend properly, to mount a proper defence against a larger force, you need air support, in this case too. However, there would have to be a threat and armed contact. And requests for air support, that was a procedure that I was involved in indirectly, not directly. In any case, we needed proof that there was effectively a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you also needed visual contact. You said: We can't see them; you wanted to see them. Was there a particular reason for that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, that was not me, I myself. However, if you have contact particularly in case of close air support, then you need to be able to see as well what's going on related to danger to your own troops or harm that you might do, damage that you might cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how many forward air controllers did you have in your battalion?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Organically we had two forward air controllers who'd been trained for this. These were their main tasks, and in addition to that there were also other people who were suitable for this, for example, special forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you had your own forward air controllers and you had some extra ones. Under whose control were the extra ones?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all under the battalion commander's command, so that was Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it for the sake of forward air controllers that you needed to see the troops and the artillery, so they can guide air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I said before, a forward air controller in a case like this must truly see the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So he's practically aiming for the airplane above and he makes up part of the crew of the airplane; right? I'm afraid there's a problem with the transcript. Just give me a moment, please. So the forward air controller is working together with the crew of the aircraft, aiming the fire; right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, joint -- jointly, they have contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me this: You were talking about the 10th of July. You said there was shooting around the road that was crawling with refugees. Was it direct or indirect fire? What were they firing with, mortars? A cannon maybe? With direct visual contact? Or was it a tank? What kind of shells were they?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a complex question. As far as I can recall, on the 10th of July there were actual shootings, firing with -- sporadically mortars, and also indirect fire using, as I assume, a type of cannon or artillery, so indirect fire I would say. As far as direct fire is concerned, you would hear this taking place, you would hear fire. However, I have -- I did not personally observe this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that the version prevailing here was that one shell at Markale killed dozens of people and another killed just a few less, whereas you saw only one wounded boy. Could you make up your mind, were they just poor shooters or poor marksmen, or was it perhaps the case that they were not firing at the column at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, one, it's a compound question; two, I don't know what the witness is supposed to do with the comment: "Do you remember that the version prevailing here was that one shell at Markale killed dozens of people..." which has had nothing to do with his testimony, and it's argumentative as well about him making up his mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please reformulate your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Considering there was fire from both sides of the road on which there was a large number of refugees and you saw only one wounded boy, were you able to conclude that they were poor marksmen or perhaps they were not aiming at people at all?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we speak of both sides of the road the way you're indicating, I indicate of the 10th more from the city, inside Srebrenica, where you're on a low point between some hills. There was quite a lot of population there in the streets and here and there mortars would land from outside the city, in the city itself. Whether the intention was to injure people, target them, or make them worried, concerned, I think the latter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Concerning your own movements and the movement of civilians, were you able to conclude that the purpose of the fire was to obstruct, not to shoot to kill?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the idea that it had more to do with the people, the Muslim population, to get them moving, to eventually get as many of them to go to Potocari as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm now asking you about the fire. I'll ask you later -- in fact, I'll first ask you about UNPROFOR. Did you observe that the fire vis-a-vis the battalion had the purpose of limiting your exit from the base and that you had no casualties?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and effectively myself, I saw a number of times shootings just behind me, both from types of tanks as well as by mortar, with the intention to make it clear that we as DutchBat had to stay on base as much as possible and not drive around too much outside. And this was also made clear to me at one time when I was in touch in one of my trips to Bratunac for a talk with some Serbian military, who indicated that, you know, we had to be careful and only relocate when absolutely necessary; preferably we would make contact, they said, through a sort of walkie-talkie system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Concerning the movement of people, were you aware that it was the authorities that got the people on the move by sending messengers to every village, that people should gather in Potocari, and it had all started long before the Serbs appeared?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I just ask if there's a basis for the part of the question that "this all started long before the Serbs appeared," that the messengers were sent out to tell the people to move to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think he cited the previous evidence. I think it's fair enough for the accused to put that question. I'll consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we can continue. Can you answer the question, Mr. Boering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me try to assist the Chamber and Mr. Nicholls. It was explained by the previous protected witness. They didn't even know what was going on until the authorities came and said people were moving towards Potocari.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 65 ter 19721 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is our case that there was no threat and no danger to civilians and that the civilians, based on their own evaluations and their own fears, gathered in Potocari. Is that correct? This document relates to the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please wait. You put your case to the witness and please let the witness answer the question. Just wait. You heard the question, Mr. Boering. Not relating to the document, Mr. Karadzic put his case that there was no threat and no danger to civilians and that the civilians, based on their own evaluation and their own fears, gathered in Potocari. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were there any contacts in town between the civilians and the Serb army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One at a time, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not agree with what Mr. Karadzic says. There was effectively fear among the population and they didn't have a clue as to what to do. I myself walked among them and talked with them several times, and they asked me what they were supposed to do, and that included people I had known for a long time and I had good contact with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was not very adept in putting my question. My question was supposed to mean: Was there any contact between Serb infantry and the civilians in town itself, or had the civilians gone to Potocari even before?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself, the last two or three days before the enclave fell in Srebrenica, the view on Potocari, I do not have an idea for the last one and a half day. However, I didn't think there were a lot of people on their way to Potocari. I think it was more a gathering around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was anyone threatened by guns in Potocari? And look, please, at this document that starts with some rumours about people held at gunpoint and then later it was ascertained that that hadn't been the case.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Threatened, guns in Potocari -- I'm not sure what you're talking about. By whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am trying to say that even -- look at this document. It says guns were being pointed at people, at least that was said, and then it later turned out it hadn't happened. Even you confirm it hadn't happened.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I can see it, this report was drawn up when the enclave had already fallen. The flow of refugees had already gone to Potocari, and effectively there were a number of Serbian soldiers walking around at the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what I'm asking you about, the situation in Potocari. Were these civilians at gunpoint or threatened by weapons or is the situation as described here, that the situation was normal as regards Serb soldiers? I can actually read this out in English and then it can be interpreted. [In English] "They also went further to surround the prefab factory about 200 metres from the compound in the direction of Potocari where there are also a large number of refugees. UNMOs were asked to talk to some BSA soldiers who were said to be pointing their guns in a threatening manner at the refugees in the prefab factory. However, this proved to be false when we got there. Contrarily, we observed some of the BSA soldiers giving out cigarettes and candies to a few of the refugees. Hope this would not prove to be a deceptive act, though." [Interpretation] So you did not observe that they were threatened in any way, by weapons, that is?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read the report, which was probably drawn up by UNMOs in that same period. I also asked a few UNMOs to go and stand near a building where men were selected, deported, and they were effectively threatened with guns. The report, as I read it here, I cannot judge, I do not have any such observations. But I did see another event at the same time, probably involving members of the same team of UNMOs. However, if I remember the name correctly, they were present under Kingori.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1969, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So at the time you had not seen a single killing, whereas you and your fellow officers saw nine bodies by the well, but you did not see how and when these people had lost their lives; right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at 65 ter 02003.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Drina Corps, July 13th, and it says 200 to 300 enemy soldiers managed to get to the area of Mount Udrc and that there is fighting there. And then paragraph 3 says that: "The Corps zone of responsibility is under full control. So far from the Srebrenica enclave about 15.000 Muslims were transferred in an organised fashion." That is probably the regular combat report for that day. Did you hear shooting? Did you hear about this happening around Srebrenica, in the mountains and forests?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I've understood, there were a number of Muslim military who left the enclave in order to try and reach Tuzla. It was unclear to me how many there were. However, at any rate it must have been most of the military in possession of weapons because there weren't a lot of men among the refugees around Potocari. When I left with the first transport, the first refugees, the first convoy - perhaps 10, 15 buses - the route that we took we stopped twice because there was firing. I assume from people fleeing to Tuzla, and that had to be solved by the Serbs -- Muslims, Muslim people fleeing to Tuzla. That is my recollection of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued]... the last page. Can we have the last page, please. "Decision" in English. Please take a look at what General Krstic's decision was on the 13th of July. Effect control over the territory, disarm, disperse Muslim forces, protect the population and property and at the same time secure the lines of defence from attacks from behind. Parts of the forces, et cetera. Do you see that even at that time General Krstic said that the population should be protected and that was one of his major points?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I'm reading here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge to that effect? Does this sound plausible to you as proper conduct on the part of a military commander? Is that the way one does behave?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is what one could describe as good behaviour, the correct way of acting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1970, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly have a look at 65 ter 01983.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this, this is an order. And when describing the enemy it says, paragraph 1: "The enemy in the Srebrenica enclave has completely been routed. The terrain is being cleaned up." And now could you please turn to page 3 so that we can see 9(c) in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Next page in English, please, and third in Serbian. (C) "Security."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the paragraph down here. [As read] "The civilian Muslim population and UNPROFOR are not targets of our operations. Collect them together and keep them under guard, but crush and destroy armed military groups." Was that what was done?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you a complete view on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, are you asking the witness about the Zepa operation or in relation to attack against Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, from the point of view of the Drina Corps, these were two enclaves that were together. This is an order that had to do with the treatment of the population and UNPROFOR with regard to both Zepa and Srebrenica. It's a strictly confidential document, a military secret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You heard the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Are you going to have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you have another opportunity to tender this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I agree. 65 ter 02023.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Boering, that this is only the 12th of July when they started providing fuel. It says: "Pursuant to the order of the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska to provide 50 buses for evacuation from the Srebrenica enclave, we hereby request you to approve an additional quantity of fuel ..." and so on. And then buses will be used from the municipalities of Pale, Sokolac, et cetera. And it says their final destination is unknown so far. So the commander of the Drina Corps, as he is leaving, he does not know where the refugees will decide to go. And it's only on the 12th that the fuel and buses are being prepared after General Mladic had received information from the Muslim leadership as to what it was that they wanted; right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the date the 12th of July on this document. And on the 12th around the lunch break, 12.00, in Potocari I did see quite a few buses for the first convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1971, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Boering, that on the 13th in the morning the buses were being boarded even before the Serbs appeared?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. I was not there anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, that's right. You had left. However, let's have a look at 65 ter 2352. Do you agree that this is a report pertaining to the 12th of July, probably just before dark, where it says: "The transport of the refugees has stopped because of the dark. Tomorrow morning at 0700 hours it will start again. [In English] The refugees were dropped about 4 kilometres from the confrontation line with Tuzla. They were treated good and no one was harmed. This was stated by one of the DutchBat soldiers who escorted the convoy. "We have no more news ..." and so on. [Interpretation] You were with one of these convoys that was going towards Kladanj; right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was with one of the convoys, the first. What happened with the other convoys I do not know personally. For the first convoy in which I myself was involved, I did see that upon arrival at the point from where they had to go on, on foot, men were singled out, taken apart into the woods, and I was not allowed to follow them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is it correct, Mr. Boering, that they did not walk from the confrontation line to Tuzla; rather, only to Muslim-controlled territory?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, some witnesses who were part of foreign troops said that they were brought to -- close to the confrontation line and that then they walked to Tuzla, all the way to Tuzla, whereas I believe that they only walked across no man's land. Tuzla is very far away. Would you agree that they walked only 3 or 4 kilometres and not the entire way to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a walk of around 4 to 5 kilometres, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1972, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's time for you to conclude, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct - and it's in 92 ter, that is to say your testimony in Popovic - you said that you were not particularly welcomed in Kladanj, that is to say by the Muslim side; is that right? They did not trust you and they treated you in a hostile way; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Boering. My time is up. Thank you for your kind answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Boering -- Colonel Boering. You were asked yesterday quite a bit about firing on the population, that's 22124, as well as today in the time before the -- and during the time that the civilian population of the enclave all went to Potocari on the 11th. You were asked yesterday at 22086 about negotiations that were said to be the reason for why all the people decided to go to Potocari and to leave, including Mr. Akashi and the Muslims. And there was also a discussion about -- 22122, about what date this was, whether this was the 8th or the 11th of July and whether there was shelling at that time. And you were asked more about that today. So I just want to go over a few documents from that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 02342, please, 65 ter number. And if we could blow that up so that the Colonel can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is an UNMO report from 10 July at 1338, so in the afternoon. And could you just look - it's brief - at the paragraph, Colonel. "Subject: Situation update. "Srebrenica township is still undergoing a very heavy shelling. So far we have recorded figures 49 shells since 1250 hours to 1353 hours this afternoon with a figure of 9 rockets launched into the town ..." And then it goes on: "We estimate the current situation to be getting worse, still monitoring." Can you comment now --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? May I ask Mr. Nicholls not to skip this part --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that says "exchange of fire."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine. "Rockets launched into the town and exchange of occasional HMG and SA firing. We estimate the current situation to be getting worse. Still monitoring."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, reading this paragraph, can you comment on its assessment of the shelling in the town of Srebrenica on 10 July?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And as well as the meaning of HMG and SA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, which I have to confess I'm not sure of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] HMG is heavy machine-gun. SA is small arms, you know, hand weapons or repeat weapons, repeat guns. And this report described how effectively the firing on the enclave took place, and that it wasn't a limited quantity of fire, it was rather more extensive. And the UNMOs in their official capacity had as one of their tasks to count and report this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would tender that document, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3991, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Same topic, Colonel Boering, I'd like to move now to 11 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I please have 02346, another UNMO report from the afternoon. Can we blow that up a little bit so that Mr. -- Colonel Boering can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll just read a bit of it or as much as Mr. Karadzic wants read as well. "At this moment the stream of refugees and wounded is incountable anymore. We figure that a total of 20.000 refugees came to the DutchBat compound of Potocari already and is growing steadily. Since our last report the shelling of the town has been going on despite of the air-strikes. The town is in the hands of the BSA by now and the latest ultimatum given by the BSA is that if the air-strikes continue everything inside the enclave will be bombed. Also UNPROFOR and the other UN organisations. "B Company has left their compound in Srebrenica ... BSA," I'm not reading verbatim, "... is all around in the enclave." I'll skip a sentence. "The air-strikes on the north part of the enclave have not been taken place up till now. That means the compound is a very easy target for all the weapons on the north ridge of the enclave." And we saw in Mr. Karadzic's cross-examination the report about Commander Karremans, where he talked about the sitting duck position. Again, can you tell me -- we've had questions about the situation in the enclave and a portrait painted on the cross-examination. Can you tell us a comment on this report and how it reflects the situation on the 11 July around the compound in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report as I read it here -- yes, I agree completely with what it says here and I also recall that effectively from the part of Mr. Mladic it was indicated at one of the talks that if the air-strikes were to continue, he would not have a problem bombing us -- the enclave including us, I should say. And that this really happened on the north side of the enclave, that there was enough possibility to have targeted fire on Potocari aimed from there is something I also know. There were people firing up in the hills and they were effectively firing on Srebrenica and the environment. So the positions of a number of structures that they'd erected for that there were known to us. We knew also of the possibilities that they would fire at us from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this is before your first meeting with General Mladic that same day, is that right, that this report comes out?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I look at the time, yes, then that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I tender that, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3992, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a couple more documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 02347, please, another 11 July UNMO report a little bit later in the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I won't read it all out to save time, but it talks about the amount of water left for all the people and DutchBat, the amount of food available, that the number of severe wounded is 35 and number of light wounded is uncountable. DutchBat can't give much help and neither can MSF. Same question: Can you look at this and tell us if this -- your position on how this describes the situation as you remember it from 11 July at the compound?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This reflects the picture of the situation at the time. And if I look at the times, this was around -- this was sent around 4.00, so even before there was that meeting with General Mladic -- the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is in evidence as Exhibit P841.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh, that's right. I'm sorry. All right. Last one, 02348, again from 11 July, still talking about the situation at the compound in Potocari and the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is now about 5.00 p.m. The number of severely wounded has grown to 50, I'll paraphrase to save time. "DutchBat is trying to do something about the food situation but there isn't enough for more than 48 hours. The battalion has the intention to try to create a very small safe area (the compound?) to protect the refugees." And then if you look at paragraph 3 as well. Talking about BSA firing, that's VRS, 22 rocket shells from Dugo Polje and the co-ordinates and the sound is very close so the panic amongst the refugees increases with every shell. The same question: You talked about how you thought the shelling was to frighten the refugees, the civilians. Can you comment on this document and the situation it describes shortly before your first meeting with General Mladic, to talk about what would happen to the people?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may interject. It would be fair if Mr. Nicholls would say the witness where these shells were fired at because it says here that there is a large number of people involved in fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think the witness can read the document, which I've asked him to, and explain and will know more about where the shelling -- than I can put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document describes that at various locations there was firing, indirect firing, and that this effectively scared even more the population and the refugees who were uncertain of what is happening. So it describes the situation as I, myself, actually experienced it. And this contributed to the population who thought that they might still seek some sort of security in and around Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Right before that. Mr. Karadzic, where does this document say that large number of people were involved in fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Excellencies, it was stated in the previous document, i.e., that a large number of Muslim fighters were involved in combat. We quickly moved to a new document, hence my error. Therefore, my objection here is that no military reason has been stated here for fire to be opened at Budak and other places or whether it was for the purpose of intimidation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, this is not a proper intervention. This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3993, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Earlier today, towards the end, Mr. Karadzic asked you about - and this is at page 11 going on to page 12 - about General Krstic and showed his 13 July report and put it to you that it reflected proper conduct on the part of the military commander, specifically referring to a section about protection of the population, suggesting to you that this was the -- I believe the Muslim population and not the Serb population in that report. I would like to show you a report from General Krstic, Drina Corps commander, at this point to the Main Staff from four days later, 17 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 65 ter 02007, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can see it's 17 July and if -- I want to focus on the bottom of the page in English, paragraph 3, it's all there on the Serbian. Just take a moment to read it because I don't think you -- I'm sure you haven't seen this before. This paragraph is entitled: "The Territorial Situation in the Zone of Responsibility," of course of the Drina Corps. "The territorial situation in the Corps is under the control of our units, although complete security has not yet been established in the perimeter villages, from where the enemy are retreating ..." and it describes that and talks about an evacuation. And now I want to go to the bottom and then we'll need to go to the next page. [As read] "In the last three days, following the transportation of the civilian population from the former Srebrenica enclave to Kladanj, there have been increasing instances of women who have been allegedly -- who have allegedly got lost, coming back towards us from Kladanj and arriving at our forward line of defence. After being warned by our soldiers, they tried to run away. Yesterday two women arrived from Kladanj direction at the 1st Vlpbr's defence line in the Luka sector. As they refused to surrender and began to run away towards Kladanj they were fired on and died as a result." And I won't go through the rest of the report. As a current serving officer in the military, civilian refugees get lost and walk back towards the Serb line, General Krstic's solution is to warn them to surrender and then to fire upon them and kill them. Can you describe, does that -- I'll ask you the same question as Mr. Karadzic: How does that reflect on proper commander behaviour and officer behaviour? And there's an objection so please don't answer yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The objection is that this does not properly arise from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just Mr. Nicholls referred to this certain passage in General Krstic's order on 13th of July, so how would you respond to that argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because this document is now dealing with an incident on the 17th of July, far removed from anything that was discussed by Dr. Karadzic in his cross-examination. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm sorry. When I asked Mr. Karadzic how that document in relation to Zepa relates to the Srebrenica enclave, and then he said it's in general vis-a-vis the civilian population. So why can't the Prosecution not tender this document to rebut that argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because it raises an entirely new incident that wasn't part of the cross-examination. If you make the definition so broad that any action towards the civilian population that occurred within the month of July, for example, would be -- arise from the cross-examination, then it gives the Prosecution an unfair -- it opens the door too wide for extending the cross-examination -- the re-direct examination and seeking re-cross-examination. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I may reply, if I need to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just put a pause. Yes. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, the question regarding the 13 July document was clearly put with the purpose of showing that General Krstic was a good, professional commander, and it was clearly put that part of that was his protection and care of the civilian population and implied that that was the Muslim population he was talking about. This is four days later, it's the same people, refugees, women, civilians from Potocari; it's the same commander. When these women who were transported or got lost walked back towards the Drina Corps line, Krstic reports that their policy is to ask them to surrender and then kill them. So I think it arises directly out of the door which was opened. It's not a stretch. And when you open a door on cross-examination on -- then you have to accept the consequences.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have an opportunity to clarify what Mr. Robinson doesn't know about. This happened 60 kilometres from Srebrenica and four days after the completion of the evacuation. And thirdly, this was not a decision of General Krstic. He was simply reporting on what had happened. He didn't have information, he didn't have time to order for them to be killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that happened on the line far away from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls didn't say that General Krstic ordered that. We agree with the observation by Mr. Nicholls, which it relates to the same -- similar time-frame, it relates to the same people, it's perfectly legitimate to raise this issue. This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3994, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Excellency, Mr. Nicholls said that that was the solution offered by Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, I don't think the witness answered the question, though, that I put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, yes. My apologies. Yes, if you remember the question, could you proceed to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My question was: Having read this, how does that reflect, this report as you read it, reflect on proper commander behaviour, officer behaviour?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what's described here is a so-called war crime and an UNPROFOR commander should act against that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be given two minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know what it is, but I object straight away. This is a recurring theme of always wanting to ask more questions. I'm sorry to jump the gun, but I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it's related to this document, the Chamber is not minded to allow you to put additional questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, it refers to the previous documents where localities were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you put that question, could the Chamber hear your question first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested to hear whether the localities that were the targets were inside the town itself within the enclave or were those hills that were under the control of the remnants of the Muslim army. There was mention of some co-ordinates, and I would like to hear whether they pertain to the town proper or were they situated around the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll allow you to put that question, but if the Prosecution is minded to re-examine on that issue we'll allow that also. Put one question at a time, one by one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- yes, just one question. Further cross-examination by Mr. Karadzic:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Boering, is it correct that Gradac and Budak are not situated inside the town itself, but rather outside the town on the surrounding hills and that at the time they were fully packed with the remnants of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, as far as the second part of your question is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he didn't answer the question. Are those localities in the town or outside of the town? The answer was avoided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you -- can you answer that question, Colonel Boering?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not in the town, but near the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just one question arising from that. Further re-examination by Mr. Nicholls:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, were shells fired over the compound?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one minor question from me, Colonel Boering. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's about your rank. Did you say that your current rank is lieutenant-colonel or colonel?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's lieutenant-colonel. In the past, every now and then, I did see "Colonel" mentioned in the reports; however, my title -- the title is often mentioned as "Colonel" instead of "Lieutenant-Colonel."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies all. That concludes your evidence unless my colleagues have questions for you. Thank you on behalf of this Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole for your coming to the Tribunal yet again. Now you are free to go, but we'll rise all together. We'll take a break now for half an hour and resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Mr. Registrar, may we have 65 ter number 90299, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What is your name?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: My name is Evert Albert Rave.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And have you retired from the Royal Dutch Army?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, I retired in 2009.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What was your rank when you retired?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I retired as a major.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You've testified in the Krstic case in 2000?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In the Tolimir case in 2010?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And an amalgamated statement was prepared containing the relevant portions of those testimonies and your OTP statement from 1998. This statement, which is on the screen now, you reviewed and signed on November 10th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Because both of you are speaking the same language, please put a pause between the question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. This is time now you can -- French translation has just been completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the statement accurately reflects an amalgamation of your previous testimonies and your OTP statement?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, it reflects.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, and if you were asked today about the same matters contained in the statement, would you provide the same answers to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I would provide the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender the statement and the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3995, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm now going to read a summary. Warrant officer 2nd Class Evert Rave was deployed to the Srebrenica enclave in January 1995. As liaison officer, he kept contact with the Muslim population inside the enclave and the VRS outside the enclave. Rave also acted as advisor for field security to the DutchBat commander. From late March 1995, the Bosnian Serb forces increasingly restricted humanitarian aid convoys to the enclave. Consequently, the Muslim civilians in the enclave had insufficient food and supplies and there were instances of Muslim civilians raiding the DutchBat garbage dump. DutchBat was also affected by the restrictions. There were problems with diesel and food supplies and with obtaining leave clearances. Rave felt as if they were kept prisoners in the enclave. On the 3rd of June, the Bosnian Serbs took OP Echo on the southern border of the enclave. In the first week of July, the tensions mounted and the shelling from VRS positions intensified. Starting on July 6 and continuing the following days, the VRS attacked the enclave with rocket-launchers and artillery fire. Rave witnessed impacts in the vicinity of the UN compound in Potocari. Several civilian houses were hit. Reports indicated that civilians were wounded. Rave described the attacks on other UN OPs during the following days. The captured DutchBat soldiers from the OPs were brought to Bratunac. On July 9th the shooting intensified in the vicinity of Srebrenica and by the 10th the streets were overcrowded with anxious people. On July 11th, the town was totally overcrowded and people gathered in front of Bravo Company, the UN compound located in Srebrenica, because the people thought it would be safe. There was panic and the people were anxious and late in the morning the refugees broke through the barrier around Bravo Company and entered the grounds of the UN compound itself. Around noon a mortar shell landed between two APCs on the compound itself and there was several wounded. Eventually, DutchBat thought that the best option was to move the refugees to Potocari, as it was bigger. The witness and Major Boering left in a jeep full of refugees to Potocari, driving in a stream of refugees walking in the same direction. Mortar rounds were impacting along either side of the road. Rave concluded that the Serbs wanted to push the people to Potocari and keep them there. The UN compound in Potocari was overcrowded with about 10- to 15.000 refugees: Anxious elderly, sick, women and children included. On the 11th of July at 8.00 p.m., Rave participated in the first meeting at Hotel Fontana in Bratunac. He arrived with Colonel Karremans and Major Boering. At Hotel Fontana, the witness saw several UN soldiers who had been captured by the VRS during the take-over of the OPs. The witness was surprised to see General Mladic there. Everything in the meeting appeared to be premeditated: There was a film crew and there was no real negotiation, but it was simply dictated what would happen. The first ten minutes of the meeting were very tense. They were all put in a corner. The witness thought that the main purpose of the meeting was to show who the boss was. On July 11th at 11.00 p.m., Rave participated in the second meeting at Hotel Fontana. He arrived with Colonel Karremans, Boering, and Nesib Mandzic, who was brought as the Muslim civilian representative. Immediately after their arrival a pig was slaughtered outside the meeting room. Rave thought this to be pure intimidation, especially with Muslim Nesib Mandzic present. A camera crew was again present at the meeting. Mladic showed a broken board taken from Srebrenica government building as a trophy of his victory. At the meeting, the movement of the refugees was discussed. Mladic stated that transport would be provided, although two hours earlier at the first meeting, he asked Karremans to arrange for the buses. All plans discussed by Mladic were tentative, and at the end of the meeting the witness remained unsure as to the nature of the plans and how they would be executed. In the morning of the 12th, Rave witnessed the advance of Bosnian Serb troops towards Potocari. The advance and the continued shelling of Potocari frightened the civilians. Rave did not attend the third meeting at Hotel Fontana. After the meeting, however, Rave and Boering went back to Bratunac to discuss the details of the buses and fuel. However, upon arrival at noon, they did not find any representatives. They contacted Major Nikolic and were informed that the buses were already in Potocari. When Rave returned to Potocari at 1.00, the buses were already there. The witness thought that the entire operation of take-over and deportation of civilian population was organised in advance. In Potocari, Rave witnessed Muslim men ages between 17 and 70 being separated from the women and children. They were kept in the "White House." The witness saw several times men coming out of the house who were afraid, who tried to escape, and started screaming because they did not want to get onto the buses. These men were forced onto the buses and were hit and kicked. The witness personally saw three buses with men leaving Potocari. A DutchBat escort was stopped in Potocari [sic] and could not further follow the buses, and on the 12th the witness saw Mladic in Potocari. According to the witness, Mladic was aware of the separation process. Mladic said to Rave that they tried to find out whether there were soldiers among the men. Deportation of the refugees and separation of the men continued the next day, on the 13th, and after the 13th only wounded refugees remained at the Potocari compound. A few days later on the 16th, Rave met with a Bosnian Serb civilian who came to the compound and introduced himself as Miroslav Deronjic, the new mayor of Srebrenica. Deronjic talked about his connections with Karadzic and stated that he was in direct touch with Karadzic. Rave attended a meeting between Karremans and Deronjic. On the 17th, Major Nikolic screened out seven of the wounded, stating that they would be taken to the Bratunac hospital. Rave later heard that several wounded, maybe including the seven, disappeared from the Bratunac hospital. On July 21st, Rave and the Dutch Battalion left the enclave. Your Honours, that concludes my summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 68, you noted that you were surprised to see Mladic at the first Hotel Fontana meeting. Why were you surprised?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Well, we had never met General Mladic before and we met General Zivanovic, who was responsible for the Serbian troops around the enclave. And we had the impression that the Serbian troops around the enclave attacked us. So when we were ordered to go to the Hotel Fontana, we expected to see General Zivanovic over there because we had the idea that he was responsible so he would be the guy to meet there and eventually negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Who requested the meeting?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I really don't know, but I think that the VRS requested the meeting because I was ordered by Colonel Karremans to go with him to the Hotel Fontana. There was no agenda. We did not know what to expect over there. In my opinion, the VRS ordered the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The meeting what -- you had noted was at 8.00. What time were you told to go to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: One hour before, 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You also mentioned at paragraph 72 in your statement that the meeting seemed premeditated. Can you tell us why you think so?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Well, when we came into the meeting room, what we did not expect, of course, was, first, to see General Mladic over there. We saw a lot of civilians and a complete film and camera crew, and the setting was in that way, that we were set into a corner with no possibilities to stand anywhere else. The camera crew was filming everything. I think this is not a normal way that a meeting between two military commanders is organised, especially when the meeting proceeded the way General Mladic acted. Everything was filmed. And I think -- I had the impression that he wanted to intimidate us, but also put on the film what was happening over there. Especially at the end when we tried to leave, Colonel Karremans was ordered to drink a beer together with General Mladic. The problem was at that moment that there seemed to be no beer. What I imagine afterwards, beer is not that nice to see on a film, but when you have there a commander who won the war and lost the war and you see them toasting with a glass of wine, that even could be champagne, as you could suggest, it does it much better on the video. When I saw later on the film, and I did not realise that on that moment even the interpreter was interpreting the talks between Mladic and Karremans, was sent away a little bit because it would be better on the film to see Mladic, Karremans, focal feature, myself. So that was him -- in my way -- in my opinion enough proof that it was all pre-arranged to show the world what happened over there in the way that Mladic wanted it to show.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to show you now the video from the first meeting and it's 65 ter number 40582. We are going to start the clip at time code 33 minutes and 22 seconds. There will be a couple of occasions when I stop, but we'll watch it through.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We've stopped at 39.19, and at this point Mladic has started to speak, and he's raising his voice and we played a little bit more. But I know that you've watched this video recently. Are there other occasions at that meeting, in your memory at the meeting, where Mladic raised his voice as well?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, he did it several times. After he started accusing Colonel Karremans, he did the same after that towards me and to Mr. Boering, but I didn't see that on the film.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So the part where he is yelling at you and the Major, is that a part that is actually not on this video?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, that's not on the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We've stopped again at 39.42 and at this point Mladic says: "Who were they defending from," meaning DutchBat troops, "when nobody was attacking them?" Now, sir, at this point you had been in the enclave for about six months. Were DutchBat troops being attacked?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: At the end on the 10th and the 11th, DutchBat troops were attacked, especially on the morning of the 11th. On the evening of the 10th we had a meeting, and the question from the higher command was, of course, is there a real attack, is there a smoking gun towards the UN troops. We had to discover it. So on the next morning, on the 11th, one of our APCs went forward and was shot at by a VRS tank in advance. Also our OPs were attacked by VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And on the 10th and the 11th, were Muslim civilians also being attacked?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Already in advance because the whole enclave was attacked by mortar and artillery fire, and of course the Muslim population, the civilian population, in the enclave was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so when Mladic made this statement, was it true?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: How do you mean was it true?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When he said: Who were they defending from, when no one was attacking them?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, we were attacked. Our troops were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We've now stopped again at 43 minutes and 3 seconds, and I just should note for the record the transcript in the book 65 ter 03099 is included and at this part of the video is page 7828 of the transcript. So, Mr. Rave, here we see and we hear Mladic say: "You asked for the meeting, speak up." Now, you earlier testified that you believed that DutchBat did not ask for this meeting and that the Bosnian Serbs asked for the meeting. What do you make of this statement then?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Well, it's one of the statements of General Mladic, and for me it's just only a statement because I can't imagine that Colonel Karremans asked for a meeting and that General Mladic shows up from Pale or Sarajevo or wherever he might have been. So I think that General Mladic ordered the meeting. When he's saying now that "you asked for a meeting," for me it's just a statement and it also could be a lie. Because in the next days -- and also of course afterwards I saw that General Mladic several times lied to us on several occasions, not only for specific this meeting, but also handling with the refugees and handling with the men.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, we've just stopped at 53 minutes and 10 seconds and this is Karremans who has just said: "Not knowing that I should meet you here in Bratunac ..." And for the record of the transcript book, this is page 7834. Sir, to your knowledge, had Karremans ever met Mladic before?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, to my knowledge he never met him before.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Earlier on in this video Mladic is talking about a gentleman named Van den Broek, criticising him. Can you tell us who that was?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Mr. Van den Broek at that moment was the minister of foreign affairs of Holland.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We can continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We've stopped at 54 minutes and 28 seconds and here Karremans is mentioning Pale. Sir, can you tell us about any interactions DutchBat with Pale?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Well, we had not interactions ourself with Pale, but everything we wanted to do in the enclave, either have a leave convoy to go out, convoys to come in, supply convoys to come in, evacuations, medical evacuations, everything had to be cleared by the VRS. And every time we sent in any request, it was a request that was sent to the Bratunac Brigade most of the time via the chain of command. And they told us that they would send it to Pale. So we got the impression that everything that happened around the enclave should be approved or cleared by Pale, and I don't know if Pale was the military or the civilian authority who had to approve the clearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Karremans was just talking about his soldiers. Do you know to what he's referring?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, during the occupation of the enclave, some of our OPs were made POWs and were brought to Bratunac, and I think 20 or 30 of our soldiers who were in Bratunac as POWs.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And were they at the hotel at the time?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: They were at the hotel at that time, because when we entered the hotel we saw in one of the rooms some of our soldiers were gathered there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, that completes the video and that's one hour, 12 minutes, and 42 seconds. Now, I asked you earlier about whether there were parts of the meeting that are not included on the video, and you mentioned that there was a part with Mladic yelling at you and Major Boering. Are there any other parts you did not see on this video?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, I just make some notes. We see now several threats towards Colonel Karremans saying for -- this is not your last cigarette, do you want to see your family again? It's not -- you have only one life, you don't want to lose it here. And that was during the meeting. In the beginning when Mladic was screaming towards us, he was referring to the air-strikes, if there were any more air-strikes. He threatened us that he would target the compound, the refugees, and the soldiers that were held hostage in the Hotel Fontana.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that part is not on the video?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: It's not on the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So now we're going to talk about the second meeting. Who asked for the second meeting?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Well, the agreement was made by General Mladic at that moment. He wanted to see a representative of the civilian population at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that was only a couple hours later, correct?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, that was three hours later.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you also attend the second meeting?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I also attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And early on in the second meeting did you hear something unusual?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, when we entered the room what was not usual was that one of the VRS soldiers, and it seemed to me it was the body-guard of General Mladic, because I saw him several times afterwards near General Mladic, was standing near the window, the curtain was opened in the meeting room over there, and in the beginning of the meeting after we started, five minutes later on a pig was slaughtered under the window, and halfway the slaughtering of the pig ended, the window was closed, and the meeting went on.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is what you refer to in paragraph 78 of your statement. When the pig was being slaughtered and you heard the sound, what was the reaction of the people in the room?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Some of them did not react at all, in my opinion, because they already knew. So it might have been announced in advance what would happen. Some of them were grinning, especially the man who sat opposite to me. Later on it seemed to be Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric. He was grinning and smiling: Well, that's the way we do it. That's the way he looked.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you notice any reaction from Mladic?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You spoke earlier about your belief that the first meeting had been premeditated. Did you believe that the second meeting as well, including the pig slaughtering, was premeditated?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, of course. I think the meeting was ordered by General Mladic and -- because I don't think that he knew what representatives we would bring to the meeting. This was also pre-arranged, and especially the slaughtering of the pig was pre-arranged, just to intimidate us but especially the representatives of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to play the second meeting and this is from the trial video and it begins at one hour, 12 minutes, and 42 seconds. And of the transcript book this would begin at page 7848. We can go ahead and play that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So at one hour, 14 minutes, and 13 seconds we just heard a sound. Is this the pig sound you referred to?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. This will go on for another 30 seconds and we'll continue to play.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, how did you know that was a pig?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Well, I've heard a slaughtering of a pig -- at least the sound of a slaughtering of a pig before. My grandfather was a farmer and I heard that sound at his farm.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what -- what did you think the purpose of this slaughtering was or what was the effect of this sound?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Well, it was amazing to see the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really think I have to interject here. This calls for speculation and really there are too many questions that have nothing to do with the facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question, Mr. President. We can continue to play the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you stop it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is a bit concerned about the scheduling issue, if he has to stay tomorrow there will be no Dutch interpreters, that's what I heard. Do you follow, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I understand that tomorrow there is no Dutch interpreter, and we also have been working on that issue ourselves in order to possibly get a Dutch interpreter as well. But we did understand that the Court was not in a position to provide it. And we are also -- we anticipated that this witness was going to go, as I realise now, at least until the end of the session. We're aware of the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I followed -- noted that the witness was following in English and answering in English as well, but we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So this -- so this witness is following in English, answering in English. The Dutch issue is the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I'm concerned about this witness, Mr. Rave. My question is specifically the -- we allowed the Defence two hours. It's apparent that we cannot finish him today.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I understand. And -- I understand, Your Honour. At this point I will shorten this video and then I will have about five minutes of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Rave, just before this we heard Mr. Mladic say a comment about a sign, and this is page 7853 of the transcript. He said: "This was taken off of the Srebrenica town hall. I brought it myself." To what was he referring there?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: There was a shield, as we saw on the video, was brought in, and he just showed this as a kind of trophy, that he took it from the office now -- the building in Srebrenica, to show that Srebrenica, in my opinion at least, was his at this moment and --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And if this video continues on, you've seen it, does it then go to a conversation that Mladic has with Nesib Mandzic; correct? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And we won't watch that part of the video, but there Mr. Mandzic himself makes some statements to Mr. Mladic; right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, that's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So we're going to fast-forward and go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we going to watch it later on in any event or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It was our plan to play this video today because this witness was a participant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we play it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. We can continue to play.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President that ends the video at one hour, 38 minutes, and 7 seconds. I only have a -- three minutes of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, you had talked about how you thought the meetings were prearranged. We're now going to move to the events at Potocari. After this meeting, did you go back to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And ultimately the next -- for the next two days, did you remain at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I remained at Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In your statement at paragraph 97 you indicated that you see -- you thought the events at Potocari seemed to be organised. You wrote an entire operation of take-over and deportation of civilian population was organised in advance. That was your testimony. Can you tell us what made you believe that?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it was organised in advance because we see on the evening of the 11th that General Mladic was asking for buses. Well, we seemed to be not able to provide buses, but the next morning, on the 12th, after Mr. Boering and myself went to Bratunac again at 12.00, between 12.00 and 1.00 suddenly enough buses and trucks were available. So I think that must have been prepared in advance. Also what we saw, the separation of Muslim women and men was prepared in advance. The men were separated. Screening from the men started. As General Mladic told us, he wanted to see if there are soldiers or war criminals among them so that he could make them prisoner of war. At the end, all of them were separately brought away in buses. All the time camera crews were available to film all the events where Mladic showed up, providing bread and then candy to the local population. In my opinion, just a media spectacle. All the meetings in Fontana with the photo and film teams, as we see also in the second meeting, it was all prearranged.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And related to this, you mention in paragraph 89 that you saw regular troops and irregular troops. What about the appearance of these two groups differed?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Well, the normal VRS army was well-dressed and then well-organised. The irregular troops I'm talking about now wore parts of uniforms, wore bandannas around their heads, were just around to frighten the local population. Those were the people that stopped buses on the way to Kladanj and seized our UN vehicles. After I talked to Mladic and said that this happened, that also those troops and also his VRS troops stole flak jackets, weapons, and all those type of things from us, he told me that those were not his troops but irregular troops and he was -- they were not in his control.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So you -- and you mention in that paragraph that you thought that the irregular troops only appeared to be so. Why did you think that?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Because I can't imagine -- as we can see in the video, that General Mladic was in total control over there and he would never accept, in my opinion, that there were irregular troops acting in his area of responsibility and doing things that he didn't want to happen. For me it was just a possibility for him to give them the freedom to act badly against the local population or towards UNPROFOR and he could wash his hands and say: Well, they are not my troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. You are tendering associated exhibits, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I am, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Two of them actually? You are not tendering the video footages separately?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's correct. As I said on Monday, we hope to tender the video all at once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there is no opposition?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both documents will be admitted. Shall we give the number right now, two of them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. 65 ter number 02366 will be Exhibit P3996, and 65 ter number 15259 will be Exhibit P3997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before Mr. Karadzic will begin his cross-examination, we'll have a -- take a break for an hour and resume at 1.40. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
