utterances.text: Mr. Tieger and Mr. Karadzic, I was told through the VWS that the witness would not be available tomorrow, so I inquired of the staff whether it would be possible for another extended session after 3.00. So I was told that it would be possible. So we will be sitting till around quarter past 4.00 with a short break. That's what we can do. Please, Mr. Karadzic, please start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Does that mean it's our ambition to finish with this witness today, that it's out of the question to re-call him some other day of next week?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued]... but if necessary that may of course be possible, but I think it's more than sufficient for you to have two hours. We'll see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Rave.

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wish to thank you at the outset for agreeing to meet with the Defence and that will help us make progress more quickly today. I will try to put my question in the simplest of terms so that they can be answered with a yes or no whenever possible. To begin with, is it true that your amalgamated statement was created by the OTP and you only accepted it; in other words, is the phrasing of the paragraphs the responsibility of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, but it's a compilation of my former statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm interested in is what was omitted not what was included. Look at paragraph 5, for instance, listing your duties. However, it does not mention at all that one of your tasks was to demilitarise the Muslim army and the enclave, as you correctly stated in the Tolimir case, that's 1D04692, page 6779. You said the mission of the Dutch Battalion was - and you put it in the first place - to demilitarise the enclave, to protect and help the civilian population as much as possible along with the NGOs. Isn't it true that it was a very important part of your mission?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, it was a very important part of the mission, and I think that also in this part I can't see specifically that we had to liaise with the VRS but -- yeah, well, it is in paragraph 6. But it's also in -- part of the mission, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your interlocutors on the Serbian and Bosnian sides, and I'm talking about paragraph 6, were they aware in what capacity you maintained contact with them, did they know what your duties were?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I don't know if they were exactly aware of my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In some passages in your statements - and I can provide references if necessary, but it will go more quickly this way - you state the opinion that there was no real organised Muslim army there, there were only some independent groups; right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I didn't state, I think, that there were independent groups. The army we were talking about for us was Mr. Naser Oric and his second in command or his Chief of Staff Ramiz and some other military men known to us. But there was no standing army and we had no real visible groups in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. If I tell you that there were four brigades and one independent battalion plus a fifth brigade in Zepa and another two special purpose battalions, such as medical and another one, in total there was seven organised units with their commanders, staffs, logistics, and armed troops, would that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, it would surprise me because we never saw anything about regular, real army, as you mentioned now, and that's what I stated also in paragraph 8. We had the 8th Operational Group, but it wasn't a real group and we had no idea how the group was organised below the top of the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say "we," do you also mean your commanders, the command of the Dutch Battalion, did they know more than you did?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I don't think when we are talking about the army and the existence of a standing army, I think they also did not know that there was another organisation and which brigades that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have to clear that up a bit. When you say "standing army," you imply garrisoned units and -- that are always at the disposal of their command; right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Not only a standing army. It can also an army be that it could be mobilised, but at least I -- and I can say, we were not aware and we did not deal with parts of the army in structures like an operational group and beyond -- below that, brigades and maybe companies or even platoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that because perhaps Zulfo Tursunovic, one brigade commander, was unwilling to communicate with UNPROFOR completely?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: For me, Mr. Zulfo Tursunovic was one of the leaders of a part of the enclave. The enclave was divided, for the battalion at least, in a northern and a southern part. In the northern part we had a company commander who dealt with local leaders. In the southern part we had a company commander who dealt with the local leaders. And I don't know if we -- when we are talking about Zulfo Tursunovic, if we are talking about a military leader with a rank and even an organisation under his command. For me, he was just a local civilian leader because I also never -- I only once saw him, but I never saw him in military uniform, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But do you know that up to 85 per cent of the Muslim army in the first years of the war wore civilian clothing, that they were not fighting in uniform, they were fighting in mufti?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in your debriefing on 30th August 1995 that you had had contacts with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Bosnian Serb army, which is to say the VRS. Where did you have contacts with the ABH?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb army -- the Bosnian army, I think we're talking about the Muslims, the only contacts we had was inside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You and many of your colleagues from DutchBat have confirmed to us that you had no access to the Bandera triangle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was your access to Bandera barred by civilians or by armed civilians?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: By civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Without any weapons?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was one incident when your fellow servicemen were captured in this Bandera triangle?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, I know that in the period from the 28th of January till 31 of January, 1995, some of our patrols were stopped in the area, and the only time I was there was in the evening from the 29th of January to re-supply our own troops. I went there with Ramiz, and at that moment I've not seen there any armed men who were stopping our patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where did you get those supplies? Did you buy them from the village people or from who?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: At that moment, in January, we had still our supplies from ourselves, and of course - as I think you should know - that our supplies came from the middle of Bosnia, that were brought in by supply convoys. And we supplied our troops with our own supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now briefly look at D01956 in e-court. It originates from end January and relates to the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, is it true that your men had been captured there precisely and remained in captivity for three or four days?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: They were blocked there and were not allowed to return to the base from the 28th of January until the 31 of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at this document. There should be a translation because it's not MFI'd. It's a proper exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably it was admitted under the condition that English translation should be existing -- existent and to be uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I think that -- that was the case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have it too, but it's easier to upload I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we put it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This telegram by Naser Oric, addressed to the command of the 2nd Corps, speaks precisely to that. And it says the commander of the Dutch Battalion in Srebrenica ordered his patrols to enter the area where movement has been banned. The commander of the 281st Mountain Brigade, in agreement with the commander of the 8th Operations Group, and in observation of the agreement with the UNPROFOR liaison officer, blocked all patrols of the UNPROFOR after warning them not to move in the said direction. So this was the 281st light -- sorry, Eastern Bosnian Light Brigade in keeping -- in agreement with the commander of the 8th Operations Group. This doesn't sound like civilians. This sounds like the military, with their own structure.

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, but I also did not deny that there were military people inside the enclave. Naser Oric was one of the military leaders in the enclave, as well as was Ramiz. Of course these kind of orders from the BiH command I never saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now look at P3987.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The part for me a bit difficult to follow is that your statement that your access to Bandera was barred by civilians. Could you explain that to me? How could a civilian influence the UNPROFOR soldiers not to do something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was quite easy in that way. Of course we were aware that there were armed people in the region. What they did, they blocked us and said that we were not allowed to go in. They informed us already from the 8th or the 10th of January, when fightings were going on in the western side of the enclave, that we should not patrol there. Because it were civilians, I think that the second in command of the battalion, Mr. Franken, ordered his patrols to patrol inside the Bandera triangle, although it was not allowed by the BiH. And he ordered it because there was no army that would stop him -- at least that's what he said I think. Of course when they were stopped by civilians -- and I don't know, there might have been armed civilians, but I'm not aware of that, when they were stopped I think they stopped not to escalate the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember who they were, the civilians who stopped --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At least the civilians under the leadership of Zulfo Tursunovic, the local leader in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You've just given me cause again, very nicely, mentioning the 10th of January. Look at this where it says your access was barred by reinforcing the Buljim-Jabucno lines, and then when Serbs moved their lines, it says you were given an ultimatum to return the enemy soldiers, that is, the Serbs, to their original position. And then it says the OG 8 Srebrenica issued an ultimatum to the UN members to return the enemy soldiers to their original position, and if they failed to meet this position the command will prohibit movement of UNPROFOR in this area and take concrete steps. Now, do you remember that you were required to fight the Serbs or expected to fight the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, we were expected several times to fight the Serbs from both sides and from the BiH side as well as military as civilians as -- also from the VRS side. We frequently got the request to fight or to interfere in actions taken by one of the parties. Our problem was, of course, when Muslims asked us to interfere in the situations where the Serbs attacked and they didn't give us the freedom of movement, we had not a possibility to interfere -- intervene. The same is also from the VRS side. When they blamed the BiH attacking the VRS in the western side, so in the Bandera area, we were not allowed to go there. We also had no freedom of movement. So from both sides we got ultimatums and requests, but we were not allowed to do our job and even come a little bit in the direction to act on their requests and just -- most of the times it was to stop one of the parties fighting the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that the only demands of the Serbian side were for you to disarm and demilitarise the enclave, and they never asked you to fight their battles for them?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, but they frequently asked us to stop Muslims to fight them, because they always told us that Muslims were attacking them outside the enclave, that Muslims were fighting them. We had no possibility to go there and to check even if it was true and where they were attacking because they did not allow us to go out of the enclave. So they also asked frequently for help to stop Muslim attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that according to the agreement on the protected area, the Muslims were prohibited from launching any attacks from the protected area that should not have been happening and that tied large forces to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at P3951.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many Muslim troops do you think there were there?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: As I stated before, there were -- was no regular standing army. There were no Muslim troops but there were a lot of people in the age between -- well, let's say 20 and 50 who could have been in the army before. But there was no real army and we had not the idea that there was a standing army at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that even the wrong army can use live ammunition and even not a proper army can kill?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at paragraph 2.34, please. It was a debriefing at the Dutch ministry. It speaks of the population and the warring parties. It says around 40.000 people, including 80 per cent refugees approximately, that was in paragraph 2.33. And in 2.34 it says a combined strength of 3.000 to 4.000 men. We've heard today that you attended that meeting at Fontana, where it was said that they also had three to four tanks. And we've seen from some papers that they had been ordering tank shells. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Apologies for interrupting. As I understood, those tanks are referenced in the weapons collection point, not that they had three or four tanks. So I would say it's a misstatement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, do you know that this was established at this Dutch briefing, that they had 3- to 4.000 fighting men, four brigades with a combined strength of 3- to 4.000 men?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I was not aware that there were real brigades, and for sure not that there were 3- or 4.000 men. Of course there may have been 3- or 4.000 men in the enclave, but not that they were organised in brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many tanks they had? Did you know how many tanks they had and how they concealed them from you?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: When we came into the enclave in January 1995, before us there was a Dutch Battalion and before that, that was the first Dutch Battalion. And when they came into the enclave, there had been a Canadian Company already. And I don't know in what moment the demilitarisation of the enclave started. I know for sure that with the first battalion in the weapons collection point there were already two tanks, not only two tanks, there were mortars, there were heavy machine-guns, and lots of small arms. So in the weapon collection point were two tanks, and when we came into the enclave in January, I think in the middle of January, the first question came already from the Muslim side to hand-over the weapons from the weapon collection point, including the tanks. Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans did not allow them to take the weapons from the weapon collection point, and I'm not aware that shells for tanks came into the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, yesterday we read Naser Oric's statement here that they had five tanks and that they handed over two, or rather, handed over one and damaged another one, set it on fire. Did you know that, they had five tanks?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that from the beginning of June onwards that they refused weapons from the depot because they had more up-to-date weapons, that is what one of your officers said? Did you know that that is what one of your officers was told, that the Muslims said, "We don't need those weapons. We have better ones than that"?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, the only question heard several times during that period, that they want us to hand over the weapons from the weapon collection point. So it seems to me that they had not enough weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. So you are aware that Mr. Franken tried to get in there, that they were locked. And do you know that after that a decision was made for your battalion not to go there; right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think I have to add a little bit to that because not specifically that the battalion would not go in there, because I have it not in my notes, I think, but in my opinion we tried several times to go in there but did not succeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in the Tolimir case, 1D04698 on page 6820, you said that it was ordered that the patrols no longer go there. And you don't know whether that came from UNPROFOR or whether it was your commander who had ordered that; right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, of course our commander ordered it to our troops, and I don't know if it was his decision or it was a decision from either Tuzla or BH command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In February you were informed by General Milovanovic that he did not believe that the Muslims would honour the cease-fire. Do you remember that there was a cease-fire on at that time and it was President Carter who had mediated, he had worked this out with President Izetbegovic and myself and it was supposed to be on for four months?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, I don't specifically know about this cease-fire agreement because I think we had several cease-fire agreements. I don't know on what level and when the cease-fire agreements were arranged, and especially not this one from General Milovanovic because I even don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at 16414, that's the 65 ter number. That's not it. Sorry, 1D04701 -- sorry, just a moment, please. I am sorry. Could you please give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I assume that this was not communicated to you, but we can have a look at this document. 65 ter 16414, Milovanovic concluded that he would not observe the cease-fire. Do you know whether the Muslims observed the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, not specifically in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please cast a glance at the English version. So you were aware of the fact that the agreements signed by Izetbegovic were not being honoured by Oric; right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I don't know what agreements were signed by Izetbegovic and I don't know specifically what orders you are referring to. The only thing we know on the ground in the enclave, that as well the BiH and the VRS frequently were fighting each other, frequently were shooting at each other, and both did not respect whatever cease-fire agreement was made, because we got complaints from both sides. So if there had been a cease-fire agreement, I don't know which one you're referring to, but none of the parties, at least in our period, stick to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I leave it to the Trial Chamber now. I leave it in their hands to decide whether they're going to have this document admitted or not. It's in line with the witness's experience to the effect that the cease-fire is not observed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Witness didn't confirm anything from this document. We'll not admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, for example, the end of March 1995, Major Nikolic informed you about these problems that he had with Muslim soldiers; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I don't know which problems you're talking about now, but I can assure you that from the beginning till the end Major Nikolic from the VRS side, and of course the leaders in the enclave from the military and civilian side, informed us frequently about problems they had from each other. And I mean that frequently they asked us to stop attacks from both sides, and at the same moment both sides denied us to do our job and did not give us the freedom of movement we needed to do our job and even to try to answer their requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have a brief look at 1D04701. This is the command of this operations group, or rather, it is the Main Staff that is issuing an order to Operations Group 8 Srebrenica and the Zepa Brigade, full combat-readiness on the 17th of February, while there is a cease-fire that is in force. Do you see that his behaviour was not in accordance with the orders of the General Staff of his army, the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Well, as I said before, I was not in the line of communications of the BiH army. We did not get orders from the BiH Army, and these kind of orders I never saw before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you agree that it is the Main Staff here that is issuing an order to take measures to raise combat-readiness of units? This is being sent to the 2nd Corps command, to the command of the operations group, and particularly to the 1st Zepa Brigade command. Do you know what the 8th Operations Group was, Operations Group 8 Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page for English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I told you before, there were representatives of the 8OG inside the enclave being Naser Oric, Ramiz, and some others. That was for us the 8 Operational Group. And of course I can read what is in this order but that doesn't say anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But do you think that you would have thought if you received it at the time that he was saying this to civilians or to a military unit? Look at this, raise combat-readiness, full combat-readiness, helicopters, evacuation, camouflage, and it says here -- [In English] "Should the helicopter be found, in your contacts with UNPROFOR representative take the position that its purpose was to transport political representatives of Srebrenica and Zepa who were to take part in the work of political organs of the state ..." [Interpretation] Number 6: [In English] "The command of the 2nd Corps will carry out the preparatory activities given in the directive, in connection with the engagement of forces in the direction towards the protected areas of Zepa and Srebrenica." [Interpretation] This is a long order, isn't it? This is not being sent to civilians; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, the first question here is: If you had received it at the time would you have thought it was being sent to civilians or military units. He can't answer this question. Anyone can read this document and make some guess as to who is on the receiving end of it. But he's already indicated that he's not in this chain of command, and I don't think he's the appropriate person to try to affirm this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having heard the answer given by the witness that he only met civilians, I think the question was fair enough. Can you answer the question, Mr. Rave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I read this document, it's a document sent to a military organisation, that's clear for me. As I stated, we did not only deal with civilians in the enclave but also with representatives of the 8th OG being Naser Oric and Ramiz and some others. So there was a top and there was a part of a military organisation, but not a standing army. And -- well, that's the only thing I can add to this. And having read parts of this, as I also stated and I think we can read it in several of my statements, I have no information that full combat-readiness of other or units were prepared in the enclave. I have not the information that military actions were taken out, no military exercises were done. Now and then there were rumours or the VRS informed us that it took place, but that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the briefings in your battalion, was there any mention of helicopter flights, weapons, supplies, and so on, was there any mention of that?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: We frequently had information about helicopter flights around the enclave and not inside the enclave, and I have no information about weapons, supplies towards the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that at one point in time, as you said, you went down to 16 per cent of your ammunition reserves? What were those reserves in the beginning of January?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not in that chain of command. I only know that there was not enough ammunition that was needed because the clearances were denied to bring in reserves of ammunition or ammunition at all. And I think this is more in the line of Major Franken or Major -- Mr. Karremans to ask because I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, can you say how that happened, how come you went down to only 16 per cent of your ammunition reserves? Did you have some kind of combat action or what?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: We went not down to 16 per cent. We -- and now I'm a little bit speculating, but I know for sure that all the ammunition we needed in the enclave and that should be provided to us when we came into the enclave and that already started with the first Dutch Battalion, that the VRS did not allow us to bring in enough ammunition to do our job properly, at least to bring in the ammunition that was required to do the job properly. I taste a little bit now that you are suggesting that we had lots of ammunition and it went down to 16 per cent because either we used it - and I think your next question will be - or did you gave it to the Muslims. The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, I'm just asking what you did with the ammunition when the quantity varied. What did you do? At one point in time there must have been 100 per cent. How did it go down to 16 per cent? And this is what you said in the debriefing, 1D04697, the debriefing of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we can look at that and I'll look at this debriefing, but I think this is Mr. Franken's debriefing. And as this witness says, either way he's never said 16 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted, so can we have it removed from our screens?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, ABiH document, order by Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I was being unclear. In the beginning of this he said you said in your statement about the 16 per cent. The witness indicated: I've never said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not about 16 per cent. It's order from the General Staff of the ABiH, ordering the 8th Group to bring units to full combat-readiness.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So I understand that 4697 is not a previous statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. He's asking to tender 1D4701, and I'm asking your opinion as to its admission, the document which is before us.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. My confusion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, I was told it has been already admitted. What's the number for that? Yes, D1955.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I forgot about that. That's right. What I have here is a piece of information, that it was said in the debriefing of the 28th of February 1995, and the number is 1D04697, that you got down to 16 per cent of your ammunition. I cannot see that being ascribed to Franken anywhere. Page 4. Now we are going to look for 16 per cent. That will help us more than anything else. The first paragraph, the last line. Now let us see who said that. Perhaps that's on the previous page. Perhaps we can see there who it was who said this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First page -- if we see the first page it is a statement debriefing by the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That's why it's being cited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that this was said at the Dutch debriefing, that ammunition went down to 16 per cent, the ammunition reserves, that is?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I don't know if it states that it went down to 16 per cent. I think that the ammunition reserves were at 16 per cent. And in my opinion -- well, this -- this could be true and it's in the statement. I am for sure that we never had 100 per cent. And of course, when you plan an operation you plan 100 per cent of ammunition and other stocks, but if you've got only 16 per cent, then the ammunition reserves were at 16 per cent -- at least that's my translation from this document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, why would the Army of Republika Srpska allow you to bring in unrestricted quantities of ammunition into an enclave where you were supposed to guard a demilitarised zone and where you're not supposed to spend any ammunition?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think that you're well aware that when a military organisation is ordered to go out and do their job, they take everything they need. And one of the normal things is that you carry weapons, you also carry with that weapon ammunition. When you don't have ammunition, you don't have to take your weapon. I think that in this political side that in the beginning the Dutch army was not allowed to take in a lot of heavy weapons as they would like it themselves. So there was an agreement what weapons should have been taken to the enclave. When they went in, they were not allowed to bring -- yeah, they were not allowed to bring in all the ammunition they wanted to, and not only the ammunition, also rest of the reserves and rest of the stocks we needed were refused because clearances were not granted to bring reserves into the enclave. And it's, in my opinion, standard operational procedure that if you take your weapons you also take the ammunition you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't have an answer yet, Mr. Rave. How did these variations happen in the quantity of ammunition? What happened to that ammunition? What is written here was that this was an incident, as it were, that the ammunition reserves were at 16 per cent, that is to say that they were not always at 16 per cent. So what were you and your units bringing into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I don't know where you read that it was not always 16 per cent. I think in this debriefing the only statement is that the ammunition reserve were at 16 per cent, and I'm not a logistic officer. I really don't know if it might have been a little bit more or a little bit less. This is the information I got, and I think even at that moment this is the information, because it was current at that moment, I think the debriefing was from August or September 1995, so that might be in my memory, and I can't find anything in my notes about it. And I wasn't a logistic officer and I have no documents about it to prove if there was more or less.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page of this document. Can we focus on the second paragraph from the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that a lot of money was being smuggled in cans and that there were many, many ways of abusing the presence of international organisations, to take money into the enclave, out of the enclave, deposit it in German bank accounts. Please take a look at this paragraph from the very beginning. Let us see what Naser is being asked for. He is being asking for a million to be smuggled and then further on, this entire paragraph, until the paragraph that starts with the words "Major De Haan."

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: But what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of that, the smuggling of such large amounts of money into the enclave and by their military commanders at that? Also, they tried and probably succeeded in abusing the presence of foreign representatives there, and in this way they managed to smuggle this through the Serb ranks?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I was aware, at least it was a rumour, and it came from the former battalion, from the 12th Battalion, that Naser Oric was approaching people to bring in large amounts of money. In the first meetings we had with him I suggested, for me, to see if it was possible to get the question again because for me it was only a rumour. I was never asked and -- nor of the people in my vicinity were asked to smuggle in big amounts of money. As you have read in the first page of my statements, one of the things I was -- I was there for was the field security and one of the things in the field security for me was to take care that all the UNPROFOR soldiers were as impartial as possible to all the parties and not get involved with this kind of things. So when we had rumours or information that money or those kind of things were try to smuggle in or people were approached to bring in or use their post lines to bring in large amounts of money and then they got a request, then most of the time I was informed about it and we stopped it and it did not happen. I once was informed that one of the Dutch soldiers got a post package from Holland that contained several cans and in the cans was a big amount of money. We confiscated it, our royal military police took it. We made a report of it and it was sorted out in Holland where that came from. These were not big amounts of money from one person. This was money from a lot of Bosnian people living somewhere in Europe. They collected the money, put it in cans, put lists of names with it, and in that way they tried to get it into the enclave to provide the local population with a little bit of money so that they at least could buy things on the market.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm kindly asking you, Mr. Rave, not to feel attacked in any way, neither you yourselves nor the United Nations nor the Netherlands. I know very well what our people are capable of doing in order to cover their traces and the smuggling that they were involved in. I'm just asking you whether the Army of Republika Srpska, apart from the fact that they were entitled to inspect the convoys, that in addition to that that they had very good reasons to carry out these inspections. That was where my question was leading to. I didn't want to accuse anyone of anything. Do you agree that any army that is supposed to grant passage has the right to know whether a people bringing in something or out of the area are carrying something that might be used against this army?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, it might be the right to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can these two pages that were put to the witness be admitted, pages 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I have to add a little bit of this. Of course they have the right to check, but I don't think that when they check convoys that they are not allowed to steal from convoys to make their own choices to take out whatever they like and make their own decisions on that. Because there is no border police, there are no borders, and if they can't prove that is something that is -- could be used against them, then it should be possible. But I don't know if it's possible for them to steal, for example, clothes or shoes from UNHCR convoys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pages 1, 3, and 4 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: 1, 2, and 3 I suppose would be proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said 3 and 4, so I included the first page, the cover sheet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for the purpose of identification. So number 1, 2, and 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whatever the pages, they will be the two pages shown to the witness. We'll give the number, Exhibit D --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1973, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rave I couldn't agree more with anyone else as I can agree with you, that this was impermissible and that nevertheless these things happened. But we must state that those things were prohibited and that they were not included in the orders. Do you agree that all of this was happening due to individual acts of indiscipline?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I don't think so because most of the time when -- at least in our visibility convoys were stopped, they were stopped at the so-called Yellow Bridge, our point of contact to the VRS. And most of the time there were several soldiers under the leading most of the time of Major Momir Nikolic. So I don't think they were incidents and I don't think they were individuals who did it; it was, for me, a structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find out if there was any permission given or any order given to steal, or did it happen that at times when the command managed to locate the items, these items were trimmed. So my first question was: Did you know that there was a permission or an order instructing the soldiers to steal?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that the Serbian side, primarily Major Nikolic, tried to get in touch with Naser Oric through you and that Naser Oric refused to communicate with him?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Major Nikolic several times tried to get in touch with Naser Oric. It's amazing that it started in the beginning -- no, in the middle of March until the end of March I think, and later on it happened several times. I think that Major Nikolic was aware that Naser Oric was not in the enclave at that moment, although we didn't know. He asked us and I think he might have heard the rumour or he might be informed that he was not in the enclave, and via us he tried to get the confirmation that Naser wasn't in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, now, I'm not an intelligence officer, therefore I cannot qualify this as speculation. You cannot deny that the Serbian side tried to get in touch and that they did so in order to reduce the number of incidents. Does that sound reasonable to you?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, not at all. I think they tried to get in contact to reduce the number of incidents. I think that we, as a liaison team, we were able to speak either to the Muslims and to the VRS, were very capable to bring over messages from both sides without them letting meet each other because there was so many hatred over -- that -- I don't think that they even wanted to meet. Both sides had the idea that it was too risky to meet each other I think. So it was -- again it was played, but none of the sides wanted to meet the other one physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, the fact is that Colonel Vukovic and Major Nikolic informed you, particularly towards the end of May, the 31st of May, for example, about huge losses incurred by the Serbs and the incidents in which the Muslim army left the enclave in order to kill the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: That's correct, but then we also have to add that at that same moment we asked Major Nikolic, as we did several times before, and also Colonel Vukovic, to give us the freedom of movement, either the UNPROFOR troops or the UNMOs in the enclave, to go out the enclave and check the statements they were made. Because we only had those parts of information, those statements. They often seemed to be false because both sides blamed each other of doing these kind of things and we had not possibility to go out and check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But don't you as officers trust each other? Why shouldn't you believe Colonel Vukovic and Major Nikolic that the Serbs were getting killed as a result of the missions undertaken by the Muslim army outside of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: It's not only the officers. I think it was a war situation and we had several times promises from Major Nikolic and Colonel Vukovic about agreements we made. Several times they proved not to stick to their promises and not to stick to the agreements we made to each other. So of course you get a situation that you don't trust each other and everything that is said has to be checked, double-checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly look at 1D1961.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on some occasions the Serbs demanded vehemently for Srebrenica to be demilitarised or else they were going to launch an attack? I think the number is wrong. It should be 1D1961 and it was 1D1474. Did you hear my question? Is it true that the Serbian officers told you on many occasions: Bring the demilitarisation to the end, otherwise we are going to launch an attack?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to show you a few Muslim combat reports in which they speak about dozens of Serbian casualties inflicted by the troops from the 28th Division. For example, one of them is a report, look at the English version of it, which says and describes what members of the 28th Division were doing; inter alia, they were intensifying activities behind our lines around Srebrenica and Zepa and they are tying our forces in order to prevent us from sending them to Sarajevo front. They killed 40 people, they burned the village of Visnjica to the ground, et cetera. Don't you see that this tells you that you should have believed the Serb officers when they said that the situation had become unbearable?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Of course we got frequently disinformation from the Serb officers. We reported it, and again I only can state that we wanted to prevent it. For example, because in the same time-period we frequently got the information from the Serb officers that Muslims were smuggling ammunition from especially Zepa into Srebrenica. They asked us if it was possible for us to take care of that and to prevent it. Well, we had not enough personnel because at one moment personnel was not allowed by the VRS side to return to the enclave. We had not enough material to build new O Ps in the southern part of the enclave. So the only thing we could do was our utmost to control and observe the southern part and prevent smuggling as far as we could see it. We informed, of course, the BiH about the complaints of the Serb side, and of course they denied that those kind of things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many soldiers would you require in order to be able to control between 4- and 6.000 Muslim soldiers within the enclave, particularly the soldiers who keep changing clothes from civilian to uniforms and at the same time to keep yourselves safe from being killed in a guerilla way?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think now we're getting again in an operational situation, and I think this is a question that should be asked to the commander or second in command and not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As a civilian I can put to you that as I see it the only solution was demilitarisation, because with 10- or 15.000 soldiers you couldn't have controlled 4- to 6.000 guerilla soldiers and prevent them from killing you. Don't you agree that the only viable solution was demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And I think that for a complete demilitarisation on both sides, at least not the regular army but also civilians, I think that the UNPROFOR agreement should have been changed, for example, the possibility to search all houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you have confirmed, haven't you, that on the 1st of July you met Colonel Vukovic and that he told you and described the situation to you with regard to the enclave. In addition, he said that the Serb army had to react and to that you responded that if they reacted air-strikes would follow; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I don't know if I said it that way. I'm just looking in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that this was said - just one moment - in your written statement, 1D --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 1D04690.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6 of your statement you say that you believe that he told you that they would take the OP by force, even maybe by force. That's exactly what you said.

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, I can't find it in my notes now, but I think that's true from my recollection. They ordered us to leave the OP because they wanted to use the road on which the OP was. Eventually they would take over the OP with force, and I think that we answered in that we would try to deny them the access to the OP and that, if necessary, we would ask for close air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that this belt between Zepa and Srebrenica was occupied in an unauthorised way and that the Army of Republika Srpska was denied access to it?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that because, and I just can explain, when we came into the enclave, we got a map with a red line on it, and for us that was the border of the enclave accepted by both parties, at least that was what we thought. Of course Muslims from one side and the Serbs from the other side did not accept the red line. Both claimed a little bit more to the left or to the right. We never managed to create a situation to go with one of the parties, at least one by one, along the line to check if we were talking about the same line. And I'm not aware that the situation in the south where the OP was was not correct, because in my opinion the OP was already built there in the beginning of 1994. So for us it was just there and I don't know if there were any documents in which it was mentioned that it was not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I note the time. We'll take a break for 15 minutes. You have spent an hour and 15 minutes. You have about three-quarters of an hour, and then I think it's time for you to come to more relevant issues after the break. We'll resume at quarter past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rave, let us go to the month of July as quickly as possible. Is it correct that already in early June you noticed that the Muslims were carrying out provocations from the proximity of your observation posts with the intention of drawing you into the war?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when it started --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Rave. Could we wait till we have the French interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can continue. Yes. Please continue, Mr. Rave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I can't exactly say when it started, but after the attack on the OP Echo in the south and after that on the attack of OP Foxtrot, Muslims who gathered around our OPs and tried to get in fire contact with the VRS, tried to get the UN involved in their fire-fights, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know if it's translatable. In our language we say you hide behind a grandfather and then shoot at the bear in order to save yourself. In other words, they wanted to use you and to push you into a conflict with the Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I think that the intention was that the Serbs would fire on the OPs and they expected, of course, that the reaction would be that UNPROFOR would shoot back towards the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall hearing from someone that Arkan had been noticed in the area of Srebrenica and you nearly believed that although you couldn't verify it?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I got - and I should look at my notes - at least two times the information that Arkan was sighted in the area. One specific time was that he was seen in Bratunac, I think in the afternoon or around 12.00, and the information came from the Muslim side, the same source that provided several times that showed out to be true. For example, the building up of forces in the southern part, tanks in the southern part of the enclave from the VRS and that same source who gave us that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Only in your amalgamated statement you said that those were Ekrem and Avdo Majstorovic whereas in another statement of yours you said that those men were Ekrem and Ramiz. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Well, then I have to look in my notes to see when it was and I can take a quick look. I don't have an exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. It's not that important. We can move on. Now already on the 6th and 7th of July you saw that there was fighting going on in the Bandera triangle and you speak about that in paragraph 7 of your amalgamated statement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I can't find that in my statement now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Para 7, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, paragraph 7. [In English] "A lot of fire-fighting in the Bandera triangle and in the vicinity of the OP Foxtrot" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, probably it's page 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Para 13.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 13, a lot of fire-fights took place. We got the information from our observation posts, I think, that were on the north and the south corner of the Bandera triangle, and they informed us that they heard lots of fire-fights. And of course the information from the OP Foxtrot we got directly from the OP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have time to show you some documents that are already in evidence. Let me ask you this: Were you informed that throughout the whole of June, and particularly from the 15th of June until the end of June, a major Muslim offensive was going on in the area of Sarajevo and that the Muslim forces in Srebrenica tried to step-up their activities in order to assist those fighting in Sarajevo. Just tell me if you knew about that or not?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that this is the same Bandera triangle where you were denied access by Zulfo Tursunovic's men, whether they be civilians or soldiers, we're talking about the same location?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I don't know what location you're referring to, but we only had one Bandera triangle and that was the one in which Tursunovic was the leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly have a look at 65 ter 15584.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As a soldier, tell me, would you tolerate the fact that in every offensive operation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 28th Division becomes intensely involved and engaged with the aim of defeating the Serbian army? Would you tolerate that?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Are you asking me personally or as an UNPROFOR representative that -- if we had known this and we have been able to prevent it, I think we'd have done it. But I am not aware of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We see here what General Zivanovic, who was still the commander, ordered on the 2nd of July active combat, and he is saying where different Muslim brigades are. He says the 280th is blocking the Potocari-Srebrenica axis and the 281st is blocking the Podgaj-Borovac axis, and then the 202nd Zeleni Jadar, the 283rd Podravanje-Buci village, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see here the next paragraph says that their intention is to unite these two enclaves, to connect them from a military point of view. And we see here where the 284th is and we see what his decision is as well, the commander of the Drina Corps, what his decision was. Paragraph 3, "I've decided." And you see that Srebrenica and Zepa are supposed to go back within the agreed borders, the tactical positions should be improved, and conditions should be created for eliminating the enclave because the Serb army is constantly being attacked from it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that during your first meeting General Zivanovic said to you: Demilitarise or I will attack?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I don't think that that were the words of Colonel -- the Colonel Vukovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, General Zivanovic. This is his order.

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: And the only time I met General Zivanovic was on the -- I think the 6th or the 8th of January, 1995, during the hand-over meeting in the Hotel Fontana. At that moment, General Zivanovic told me that he had the right to go into the enclave because the enclave was his, not from General Mladic, not from Mr. Karadzic, it was his, at least the southern part. That's the only thing I know about orders or ideas that General Zivanovic had about the enclave of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Didn't he say to you during your first meeting that you should demilitarise or that he would enter the enclave?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly what he said during the nine-hour meeting with lots of history, and of course I think and I can imagine that the demilitarisation was mentioned but not specifically that we should demilitarise or he would take the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I find that before the end, I'll show you what it was that had been said to you, but now I'm going to show you -- just a moment, please. International humanitarian law, respect for that, humanitarian -- let's just find that. Just a moment, please. Oh, all right, we don't have time. I don't have time to deal with this any longer. So now let's move on to July. You saw and you received information to the effect that in the south where the enclaves touch, the Serb army is advancing; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: We got the information that more and more VRS troops collected in the southern part of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then an attempt was made to have your people withdrawn from the observation post, and then the Muslims killed a soldier of yours using a dum-dum bullet; right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. When the OP Foxtrot was taken over by the VRS, the OP manning withdrew from the OP. They went down in their APC via dirt road to the main road and that was going through the enclave of Srebrenica. At the end of the dirt road, Muslim civilians were gathered there and the soldier was killed, or by a hand-grenade or by a gun-shot, I'm not sure for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. In the Tolimir case Mr. Franken said that that was a dum-dum bullet, but all right. Is it correct that your army, or rather, your troops from this observation post decided to go ahead rather than back and to surrender to the Serbs rather than go back into the enclave, that is paragraph 34 and paragraph 35. Please take a look at your statement. [In English] "The men from the OP only had one possibility, going forward and surrender to the VRS because they were just afraid going backward where the Muslims tried to stop them and they had that incident on the same day some hours before when the soldier Raviv van Renssen was killed."

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, and what's your question? Because we're talking now not about the OP Foxtrot but the OP Uniform in the south, and we had more from that OPs -- the Muslims in the vicinity of the OPs denied us to do our military job in the way we used to do it. They only had one idea, UNPROFOR should go forward and attack the VRS in the way and they would maybe do it. We -- it was not our way of working. We were trying to go backward and find a new position somewhere else. The Muslims did not allow us to go backward so the only possibility for the OP manning was go forward and surrender to the VRS troops, and of course in their mind they knew that if they would not listen to the warnings of the BiH, there was possibility, just as happened to Raviv van Renssen, to be shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today during the examination-in-chief you confirmed the suggestion made by the OTP that your people had been taken prisoner by the Serb army. What I'm saying is what that was -- that that was their choice, to move towards the Serb army, and that after that they were put up at the hotel in Bratunac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on in the night between the 10th and 11th you did confirm, did you not, that Muslim soldiers left the enclave and tried to breakthrough to Tuzla; right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: No. In the night from the 10th on to the 11th we had a meeting in the PTT building in Srebrenica. Colonel Karremans, Major Boering at that time, and myself, to inform the local population, the civilians and the military population, about what was happening and the ultimatums that were made. When we were in the vicinity of the PTT building, we saw a big group of men gathered over there. All -- no, most of them in uniform -- a lot of them in uniforms, most of them armed with small arms, grenade launchers, and all those kinds of things, and they were walking in the north-western direction. We had no idea what was going on and at that moment we had no idea about a column trying to make a breakthrough in the direction of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Ramiz Becirovic's statement it says that at the request of the Muslim's side Karremans asked for air-strikes, although you did not have visual contact with the Serb army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: No. During that meeting at -- in the PTT building at 11.00, Karremans informed the military and the civilian leaders in the enclave that there was an ultimatum, that if attacks were going on that it might be possible that there was an air-strike. That's the information that's correct. So he informed that there might be a possibility that there was an air-strike when attacks were going on. And I think that today already stated that on the next morning one of our APCs went forward, was shot at by a VRS tank, and that was a confirmation that we were still under attack and that was the moment I think that the information went up the chain of command to ask for support.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the Muslim side, Ramiz and the rest of them, gave you co-ordinates as to where the Serbs were and that you forwarded this information to NATO, with a view to air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: No. I think that the liaison team was the only one, except on some occasions also the commander, but most of the time the liaison team dealed with Ramiz and we never got from Ramiz information about Serb positions that could be used for air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have information from your side and from the Muslim side that you acted in concert, that they had provided you with these co-ordinates and that this first attack took place before you actually saw the Serbs at all. However, if you're denying that, there will be others who will confirm it. Tell us this, please, is it correct that you did not know where they had gone on the evening of the 10th, this large armed group?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying it's not correct or is -- are you saying that you did not know?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: The only thing I know that the large group went from Srebrenica on a dirt road in a north-western direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like us to deal with this meeting a bit and that film that was shown to you. Mladic says to Karremans: You asked for a meeting, speak up. And you say that you did not expect Mladic and that Karremans did not expect Mladic. Did Karremans ask to liaise with the Serb army, not expecting that it would be Mladic though?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think the only one that can answer that question is Karremans himself, if he asked for a meeting. In my opinion he did not because when we left the enclave and we go to the 7.00 to leave or I was informed at 7.00 that we have to be in Bratunac at 8.00, that there was a meeting, but there was no agenda, that's a question for me. Because when I ask for a meeting I think I have an agenda and even a schedule for the meeting. So in my opinion, Karremans did not ask for the meeting but was ordered to go there or to come there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, sir, Karremans did not deny what Mladic had said to him. You asked for a meeting, speak up. Probably Karremans asked for a meeting but not with Mladic himself. He got Mladic gratis, as it were. Why did he not oppose him? Why did he not say: I didn't ask for a meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think at that moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it's for the witness to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe, but then he shouldn't be saying that he had not asked for one, I mean Karremans, because it turns out that he did not ask for a meeting. If he doesn't know one, he doesn't know the other either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with that, Mr. Rave, if you don't know one thing, then you don't know the other one either?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think we're trying now to go into other people's minds. When Mladic is asking Karremans why he asked for a meeting, I think at that moment we can see that Karremans' mind was somewhere else and not on those, in my opinion, at that moment, dirty details because it was not interesting at all in that moment. I think afterwards for a Court it interesting, but at that moment it was in my opinion not interesting who asked for the meeting. Because there was a meeting, I think at that moment we had a feeling that we lost the war and we had only one thing that we had to do, take care of the 25.000 refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in answer to the question by Mr. Mladic -- by Mladic, Colonel Karremans answered to the effect that he had a request from General Nicolai and national authorities and refugees. How were the DutchBat going to implement such a request without liaising with the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that when as a commander on the ground you got an order to go there to the Hotel Fontana to meet with one of the people that won you war, then you inform your chain of command. And of course I think at that moment you get the informations from -- and the UNPROFOR side and the national side in Holland what questions they have. And you take that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it mean that after being ordered by Mladic to come to that hotel he asked permission from his superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think so -- at least in my opinion that's the normal way we deal with. But as I had stated before, the only one that can answer that question I think is Mr. Karremans himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rave, do you remember that that film, 44 minutes, 55 seconds, at that point Karremans said the reason for the meeting was his intention to evacuate the civilians from the enclave -- to help the evacuation. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, not specifically in these words, but -- yeah, I can't specifically see what was on that minute in the film. But I think it might be one of the questions that he got from UNPROFOR or even maybe from the Dutch government, ask how the evacuation will take place. But again, I'm speaking now for Mr. Karremans and I don't think I'm the right person to ask this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But you're testifying about that and, perhaps this was not your intention, but everything seems to suggest that there was this forcible deportation of Muslim civilians from Srebrenica and that that was the Serb objective. What I'm putting to you is that the Serbs do not mention evacuation anywhere. And as for this presentation by Karremans of what the objective of the visit was, Mladic says: Bring me the civilians and let me hear from them what it is that they want. Wasn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, of course, but in these kind of situations you can ask several -- not realistic questions because it wasn't realistic. The enclave of Srebrenica had fallen. The town of Srebrenica was empty I think because, in my opinion, the whole population was near the compound in Potocari. So there was only one possibility: Either VRS leave Srebrenica and offer the people to go back to their houses or evacuate them. I don't know exactly, in film or a statement I read it again back that I saw that Mladic offered the local population: You have a choice, to go to the north, to the south, to the east, to the west, you can choose wherever you go. Well, there wasn't a choice. The only thing that there was was buses and trucks and a lot of scary anxious people, and you had only one goal: Get away from here. And wherever they bring us is okay, get us away from this territory where we were imprisoned for more than three years in very bad circumstances. And they only had a goal, to leave. And the not realistic question: Let us know where you want to go, 25.000 people without any leadership. The Dutch Battalion tied on both hands -- well, I think it's not an issue to discuss. It's pure unrealistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, do you have the 65 ter number of the trial video transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it printed out, but I don't have all the minute references. The Prosecution must have that, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm just asking for my reference. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can leave all of that aside. What I'm asking you now is whether it is correct that only UNPROFOR and the Muslim side were speaking about evacuation and asking for buses; whereas, the Serb side was waiting to hear what it was that the Muslim civilians wanted and they're asking to have a military representative there to agree on the hand-over of weapons there. The Serbs do not mention evacuation at all. Mladic is asking to see the legitimate representatives of the civilians to say what it is that they want, and he says that verbatim: I want them to come and to tell me what it is that they want. Mr. Karremans says both "evacuation" and "buses," whereas the Serbs do not mention that; right? We can see all of that in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'm not sure that that's an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, 1 minute, 28 -- actually, 1 hour, 27 minutes -- there is a misinterpretation, "whichever way Mladic wants it." It is actually "Mandzic." Was that your understanding as well, that what was said there, whatever Mandzic wanted, Mandzic being the representative of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: I don't know exactly the subject at that specific moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think it's noted in the transcript. It's -- I take it that the page Mr. Karadzic was referring to is the page ending with 7856, when Mr. Karremans said: "I presume that is something what Mr. Mladic can tell in terms of where ..." But the transcript indicates that he was pointing at Nesib Mandzic, not Mladic. Is that what you have in mind, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree -- you said, actually, in line 47 that Mladic asked for buses; however, buses are mentioned by Colonel Karremans, he's asking for them.

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
utterances.text: Again, I don't know exactly how it is, but in my opinion when they were talking about the evacuation Mladic asked Colonel Karremans if he was able to provide buses or UNPROFOR was able to provide buses. But then we have to look it back. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the participants can see in the transcript that Mladic does not mention buses or transport or evacuation at all. He is asking them to come and say what it is that they want; however, we don't have enough time for this. Tell us now -- actually, this is not our responsibility. I have to indicate to the participants at 1 hour, 35 minutes approximately, it says Mladic says "whatever. You can survive, or rather, stay," he corrected what he was saying, "or disappear." So the word "opstati" or "ostati." So both words have to be translated but it's two different words, he corrected himself. Another thing, Mr. Rave, how do you distinguish between the squealing of a pig when it's being caught and the squealing of a pig when it's being slaughtered? Did you see this pig being slaughtered or did you just hear squealing?

utterances.speaker: EVERT ALBERT RAVE
